## Make every test able to fail when the behaviour it names breaks

_critical · any_

**Rule.** End every test with an assertion that would fail if the behaviour in its name broke. Before you
trust a new test, check that it can fail: break the condition it checks, or assert the opposite,
and see it go red.

**Why.** A test that only renders and clicks, or asserts something that is always true, stays green while
the feature is broken, so the suite reports coverage that does not exist.

## Wait for a condition the user would see, never for a fixed time

_critical · any_

**Rule.** When the result of an action arrives later, wait for the condition itself: a query that retries
until the element appears, or a retrying assertion on the value or call you expect. Give a long
operation a longer timeout on that wait instead of a sleep before it.

**Why.** A fixed sleep is too short on a slow CI machine and too long everywhere else, so the suite is both
flaky and slow, and its failures name the assertion after the sleep instead of what never happened.

## Await every userEvent call and every expect in a story test

_critical · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Put `await` before every `userEvent.*` call and every `expect(...)` in a `.test()` or `play`
function, including assertions inside `step()` and `waitFor()`.

**Why.** Without `await` the test function returns before the interaction or assertion settles, so the test
passes while the behaviour it names was never checked, and the failure surfaces later in an unrelated
test.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
Story.test("Clicking submit calls onSubmit", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
  userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
Story.test("Clicking submit calls onSubmit", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```

## Take userEvent from the test function's parameters, never from an import

_critical · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Destructure `userEvent`, `canvas`, `canvasElement`, `args` and `step` from the parameters of the
`.test()` or `play` function. Never import `userEvent`, `within` or `canvas`. In a story file,
import only `expect`, `fn`, `waitFor`, `screen` and `mocked` from `storybook/test`; `sb` belongs in
the Storybook preview file only.

**Why.** An imported `userEvent` is not wired into Storybook's instrumentation, so interactions run outside
its timing and do not show up in the interactions panel. The failures it causes are intermittent
and hard to trace back to the import.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
import { expect, fn, userEvent } from "storybook/test";

Story.test("Submits the form", async ({ canvas }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
import { expect, fn } from "storybook/test";

Story.test("Submits the form", async ({ canvas, userEvent }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
});
```

## Set every value the test asserts on explicitly when you build test data

_high · any_

**Rule.** Build test data from a builder or factory, and pass an explicit override for every field the test
asserts on or branches on. Leave random values only in fields the test never looks at. Use named
variants (traits) for whole states such as "admin" or "inactive" instead of repeating the same
overrides in many tests.

**Why.** An assertion against a randomly generated value passes or fails depending on the seed, and a
reader cannot tell from the test which value matters. An explicit override documents the input the
test depends on and makes the failure reproducible.

## Keep the unit under test real, and change the test rather than the code

_high · any_

**Rule.** Mock only what the unit under test depends on, never the unit itself. When a new test fails, fix
the test; if the failure shows a real defect in the code, report it instead of editing the code or
weakening the assertion to make the test pass.

**Why.** A mocked or quietly patched unit makes the test check itself: it passes while the shipped code is
still broken, and the bug it found disappears from view.

## Find elements the way a user or a screen reader does

_high · any_

**Rule.** Locate elements by their role and accessible name first, then by their label, then by visible
text. Reach for a test id or a selector only when the element has no accessible identity at all,
and treat that as a defect to fix in the component.

**Why.** A test that finds a button by its role and name keeps passing through any refactor that keeps the
button usable, and fails when a user could no longer find it. A test that finds it by class name or
test id breaks on harmless markup changes and stays green when the accessible name disappears.

## Make every test pass alone and in any order

_high · any_

**Rule.** Write each test so it passes when run alone and in any order. Configure and reset mocks before each
test, and share repeated setup through a small helper function, never through a mutable variable
that tests write to.

**Why.** A test that leans on an earlier one passes in the full run and fails when filtered or reordered,
which shows up as a flaky suite whose failures point at the wrong test.

## Choose the mock by what is faked

_high · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Fake a callback prop with `fn()` in `meta.args`, a request the component sends with MSW handlers in
`parameters.msw`, a module it imports with `sb.mock()` in the Storybook preview file plus `mocked()`
in `beforeEach`, and React context or providers with decorators. Never pass a provider value as a prop
or register a module mock inside a story file.

**Why.** A mock of the wrong kind fakes something the component never touches: a `fn()` prop does not stop the
real `fetch`, and `sb.mock()` in a story file runs after the module is loaded, so the story hits the
real dependency.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
// invoice-list.stories.tsx — the component calls fetch("/api/invoices") itself
sb.mock(import("~/lib/api"));
export const Loaded = meta.story({ args: { fetchInvoices: fn() } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const Loaded = meta.story({
  parameters: { msw: { handlers: [http.get("/api/invoices", () => HttpResponse.json(invoices))] } },
});
```

## Query portal content through screen, not canvas

_high · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Trigger the interaction through `canvas`, then find the portal content through `screen`, which
queries the whole document. Use `canvas` for everything rendered inside the story root.

**Why.** Modals, popovers, tooltips and select option lists are portalled to `document.body`. A `canvas`
query never finds them, so the test fails with "unable to find role dialog" even though the dialog
is plainly on screen.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /open/i }));
const dialog = await canvas.findByRole("dialog");
```

**Correct:**

```ts
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /open/i }));
const dialog = await screen.findByRole("dialog");
await userEvent.click(screen.getByRole("button", { name: /close/i }));
```

## Attach independent checks to one story with .test(), not separate play stories

_high · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Write every independent assertion as its own `.test()` on the story that has the right args. Use
`play` only for a demo without assertions, or for one flow whose steps genuinely depend on each
other, grouped with `step()`.

**Why.** Separate stories per test multiply `meta.story()` boilerplate and fill the sidebar with copies of
the same state. Assertions packed into one `play` stop at the first failure, so one broken
behaviour hides the result of every check after it.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const SubmitClicked = meta.story({
  play: async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
    await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalled();
    await expect(canvas.getByRole("button")).toBeDisabled();
  },
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const FilledForm = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled } });

FilledForm.test("Clicking submit calls onSubmit", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});

FilledForm.test("Disables submit while saving", async ({ canvas, userEvent }) => {
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i }));
  await expect(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /submit/i })).toBeDisabled();
});
```

## Write stories with CSF Next factories, not CSF 3 objects

_high · storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Build every story through the chain `definePreview` → `preview.meta()` → `meta.story()`.
`definePreview` lives only in the Storybook preview file. A story file has no default export and
no hand-written `Meta` or `StoryObj` types. How the preview is imported and what the story file is
called depends on the framework; each framework has its own note implementing this one.

**Why.** CSF 3 objects (`satisfies Meta<typeof C>`, `export default meta`) cannot carry `.test()`, and
their types are annotated by hand, so they drift from the component's props. Mixing both formats
in one project makes every new story a guess.

## Put a React story next to its component and import the typed preview

_high · typescript, react, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Create `<component>.stories.tsx` in the component's folder. Import the preview with the alias the
project's existing stories already use (`~/.storybook/preview`, `#.storybook/preview`, …), never
a deep relative path, and build the meta with `preview.meta({ ... })`.
Export stories as `meta.story({ ... })` and let TypeScript infer every type.

**Why.** The typed preview is what makes `meta.story()` know the component's props. A story file that
imports `Meta` from the framework package falls back to CSF 3 and loses `.test()`.

**Incorrect:**

```tsx
import type { Meta, StoryObj } from "@storybook/react-vite";

const meta = { component: SubmitButton } satisfies Meta<typeof SubmitButton>;
export default meta;
export const Primary: StoryObj<typeof meta> = {};
```

**Correct:**

```tsx
import preview from "~/.storybook/preview";

import { SubmitButton } from "./submit-button";

const meta = preview.meta({ title: "Components/Submit Button", component: SubmitButton });
export const SubmitButtonStory = meta.story({ name: "Submit Button" });
```

## Pick getBy, queryBy or findBy by what the assertion expects

_high · typescript, testing-library_

**Rule.** Use `getBy*` for an element that must already be on screen, `queryBy*` when the assertion is that
it is absent, and `findBy*` (or `waitFor`) for anything that appears after an interaction, a
request or an animation.

**Why.** `getBy*` throws before a `not.toBeInTheDocument()` assertion can run, so a negative check written
with it fails for the wrong reason. A `getBy*` on content that renders a tick later fails
intermittently, which reads as a flaky suite rather than a wrong query.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
await expect(canvas.getByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
await expect(canvas.getByText(/saved/i)).toBeVisible();
```

**Correct:**

```ts
await expect(canvas.queryByRole("alert")).not.toBeInTheDocument();
await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /save/i }));
await expect(await canvas.findByText(/saved/i)).toBeVisible();
```

## Reset builder counters and random state between tests that depend on them

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When a test depends on a generated sequence value or on seeded random output, reset the builder's
counters and seed before each such test. Tests that only use explicit overrides need no reset.

**Why.** Counters and random state live as long as the builder module. A test that expects `id: 1` passes
alone and fails when another test ran first, which shows up as an order-dependent, flaky suite.

## Build structured test data with a builder, not inline object literals

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Take typed test data with three or more fields, nested objects or lists from a builder. Look for an
existing builder first and create one only when none exists; never hand-roll a factory inside a test
or story file. Primitive values and objects with fewer than three fields may stay inline.

**Why.** Hand-written literals copied across tests drift from the type and from each other: adding a required
field breaks every copy, and each test fills the fields it does not care about differently.

## Assert what the user sees or can do, never internal state or markup

_medium · any_

**Rule.** Assert on what a user or assistive technology perceives: visible text, values, enabled or disabled
state, focus, ARIA attributes, and the calls a callback received. Leave internal state, class names
that carry no meaning for the user, and markup snapshots out of assertions.

**Why.** Tests that read internals break on every refactor that changes nothing for the user, and still pass
when the user-facing behaviour is broken, so the suite stops being trusted.

## Derive the expected value from the test's own input, not a repeated literal

_medium · any_

**Rule.** When the expected value follows from the test's input, compute it from that input: the row count
from the list the test rendered, a field's value from the value the test prefilled. Write a literal
only for a value the test introduces in the assertion itself.

**Why.** A hard-coded copy of the input goes stale the moment the input changes, so the test fails for a
reason unrelated to the code, or keeps passing against the wrong number.

## Group assertions by category, not one test per element

_medium · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Per story state, write one test for the static content, one for accessibility (roles, names,
focus), and one per distinct interaction, validation rule or callback. Wrap a test in `step()` when
it has three or more phases.

**Why.** A test per text node multiplies runtime and noise without catching anything the grouped test
would miss. Grouping by category keeps a failure specific enough to point at the cause.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
Story.test("Shows title", async ({ canvas }) => { await expect(canvas.getByText("Profile")).toBeVisible(); });
Story.test("Shows email", async ({ canvas }) => { await expect(canvas.getByText("a@b.co")).toBeVisible(); });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
Story.test("Renders all expected content", async ({ canvas }) => {
  await expect(canvas.getByRole("heading", { name: "Profile" })).toBeVisible();
  await expect(canvas.getByText("a@b.co")).toBeVisible();
});
```

## Make a separate story only for a different state, not for a different test

_medium · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Create a story for each state the component can render, defined by its args or mocks. When two checks
need the same args, attach both as tests to one story. Interaction, keyboard and accessibility are
tests on these stories, never stories of their own.

**Why.** A story per check fills the sidebar and the docs with copies of one state, and the copies drift apart
when only some of them get the next prop change.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const SubmitClick = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled } });
export const SubmitKeyboard = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const FilledForm = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled } });

FilledForm.test("Clicking submit calls onSubmit", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {});
FilledForm.test("Enter submits the form", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {});
```

## Give a purely presentational component stories, not invented tests

_medium · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** For a component that only renders its props (a card, a badge, an avatar), write one story per
visual variant and no `.test()`. Add a test as soon as the component has behaviour: a callback, a
conditional branch, a keyboard interaction or an ARIA state.

**Why.** A test that re-reads the text a story was given checks the args, not the component, and doubles the
upkeep of every copy change without ever catching a bug.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const SuccessBadge = meta.story({ args: { intent: "success", label: "Paid" } });
SuccessBadge.test("Renders the label", async ({ canvas }) => {
  await expect(canvas.getByText("Paid")).toBeVisible();
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const SuccessBadge = meta.story({ args: { intent: "success", label: "Paid" } });
export const WarningBadge = meta.story({ args: { intent: "warning", label: "Overdue" } });
```

## Derive a story variant with Story.extend instead of copying its config

_low · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** When a story differs from another only in a few args or parameters, derive it with
`Story.extend({ args: { ... } })` and set only what differs. Keep shared defaults in `meta.args`.

**Why.** A copied story config drifts from its original on the next change, and the reader has to diff two
blocks to see what makes the variant different.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const FilledForm = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled, layout: "wide" } });
export const FilledDisabled = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled, layout: "wide", disabled: true } });
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const FilledForm = meta.story({ args: { defaultValues: filled, layout: "wide" } });
export const FilledDisabled = FilledForm.extend({ args: { disabled: true } });
```

## Label the phases of a long story test with step(), and only of a long one

_low · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** When a story test or a `play` function has three or more phases, wrap each one in
`await step("<phase>", async () => { ... })`, taking `step` from the test function's parameters.
Keep tests of one or two lines without `step()`.

**Why.** Comments do not show in the test output, so a failure in a long flat test points at a line number
instead of the phase that broke; wrapping a two-line test adds nesting and says nothing.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
FormStory.test("Submits valid data", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args }) => {
  // fill
  await userEvent.type(canvas.getByLabelText(/email/i), "ada@example.com");
  // submit
  await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i }));
  // verify
  await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
FormStory.test("Submits valid data", async ({ canvas, userEvent, args, step }) => {
  await step("Fill the form", async () => {
    await userEvent.type(canvas.getByLabelText(/email/i), "ada@example.com");
  });
  await step("Submit", async () => {
    await userEvent.click(canvas.getByRole("button", { name: /sign in/i }));
  });
  await step("Verify", async () => {
    await expect(args.onSubmit).toHaveBeenCalledOnce();
  });
});
```

## Name stories after component states and tests after behaviours

_low · typescript, storybook@>=10_

**Rule.** Name each story after the state it shows, as a bare state name (`EmptyForm`, `FilledForm`,
`Loading`); add a `State` suffix only where the bare name would shadow a global (`ErrorState`). A
component with a single story gets `<Component>Story` plus a `name:` field, so it does not collide
with the imported component. Never name a story after a behaviour (`ClickTest`): that is a test. Name each test as a sentence describing one behaviour. Write titles
as space-separated words grouped by area (`"Components/Country Select"`,
`"Features/Invoices/Invoice Table"`), following the grouping the project's stories already use.

**Why.** Generic names say nothing in the sidebar or in a failing CI line. A failing test called "Shows
validation error on empty submit" tells the reader what broke without opening the file.

**Incorrect:**

```ts
export const Default = meta.story({});
Default.test("Test 1", async ({ canvas }) => {});
```

**Correct:**

```ts
export const SubmitButtonStory = meta.story({ name: "Submit Button" });
SubmitButtonStory.test("Disabled button prevents submission", async ({ canvas }) => {});
```
